extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, in-house counsel, and expert witnesses involved in patent infringement cases
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing whether proffered expert testimony in patent litigation meets the Daubert/Fed. R. Evid. 702 standards for admissibility, with focus on oversight of testing, potential bias, and use of evidence from co-pending litigation. The guidance explains common grounds for challenging expert reliability and admissibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal Rule of Evidence 702 requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A witness who is qualified as an expert by knowledge, skill, experience, training, or education may testify in the form of an opinion or otherwise if: (a) the expert's scientific, technical, or other specialized knowledge will help the trier of fact to understand the evidence or to determine a fact in issue; (b) the testimony is based on sufficient facts or data; (c) the testimony is the product of reliable principles and methods; and (d) the expert has reliably applied the principles and methods to the facts of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This enumerates four discrete admissibility requirements—qualification/helpfulness, sufficient facts/data, reliable principles/methods, and reliable application to facts—which courts use as a framework when performing Daubert gatekeeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daubert gatekeeping: relevance and reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: The trial judge has a 'gatekeeping function' to ensure that any and all scientific testimony is 'not only relevant, but reliable.' (Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharm., 509 U.S. 579 (1993); Carlson v. Bioremedi Therapeutic Systems, Inc., 822 F.3d 194, 199 (5th Cir. 2016)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts screen proffered expert evidence for reliability using established scientific and legal principles; gatekeeping focuses on whether methods and principles underlying testimony are reliable and relevant to the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert oversight or supervision of testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an expert has not overseen or supervised testing of accused products, the Court may properly exclude evidence based on those tests; experts must present a basis for their opinions beyond shallow conclusions drawn from test results over which they provided no oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts look for evidence that the expert guided, directed, or verified testing. Lack of oversight undermines the expert's ability to testify to the reliability of tests. See Hathaway v. Bazany, 507 F.3d 312 (5th Cir. 2007); Viterbo v. Dow Chem. Co., 826 F.2d 420 (5th Cir. 1987).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to attest to testing methodology and circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: An expert must be able to inform the court how testing was performed, who performed it, the exact circumstances observed, and other important information underlying the test results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the expert cannot verify methods, personnel, or conditions of testing, the testimony may lack the necessary reliability. Courts have excluded testimony where the expert could not validate or assess the basis for assumptions. See In re: Taxotere, 26 F.4th 256, 268 (5th Cir. 2022); Moore v. Ashland Chem., Inc., 151 F.3d 269, 276 (5th Cir. 1998).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective, independent validation of the expert's methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: The presenting party must provide 'some objective, independent validation of the expert's methodology' to show the expert's findings and conclusions are based on the scientific method and therefore reliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objective verification prevents an expert from being merely a conduit for party-favorable results. The court looks for independent corroboration or validation of the methods used to reach opinions. (Cited: In re: Taxotere; Moore v. Ashland Chem., Inc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of improper bias and use as a 'mouthpiece' for party testing
rubrics_metrics.description: An expert should not serve merely as the mouthpiece of a party's own testing or evidence; presentation of party-performed testing is ripe for bias and must be carefully considered before admission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators of improper bias include: expert had no input in testing, merely received results and reiterated them; failure to inquire into identities/experience of those who performed testing; failure to verify testing circumstances. Cases: Wi-LAN Inc. v. Sharp Elecs. Corp., 992 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2021); Dura Auto. Sys. of Indiana v. CTS Corp., 285 F.3d 609 (7th Cir. 2002); Greger v. C.R. Bard, Inc., No. 4:19-CV-675 (E.D. Tex. 2021).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability requires methodology, not just conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating Daubert challenges, courts must focus 'on [the experts'] principles and methodology, not on the conclusions that [the experts] generate.' (Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharm., 509 U.S. 579, 594 (1993)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The admissibility inquiry is about whether the opinion rests on a reliable foundation; correctness of the conclusion is not the gatekeeping standard. See Scrum Alliance, Inc. v. Scrum, Inc., No. 4:20-cv-227 (E.D. Tex., Apr. 30, 2021).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of unsupported conjecture and mere credentials
rubrics_metrics.description: An expert's personal assurances or credentials and subjective opinion alone are insufficient; reliance on 'a host of unsupported conjectures' or saying 'it is so' without methodology is inadmissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have excluded testimony based on unsupported conjecture or conclusory statements lacking a demonstrable methodology. See Hathaway v. Bazany, 507 F.3d 312 (5th Cir. 2007); Viterbo v. Dow Chem. Co., 826 F.2d 420, 424 (5th Cir. 1987).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on using co-pending litigation/testing as proof of lack of non-infringing alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempting to use testing or litigation outcomes from co-pending cases as evidence that non-infringing alternatives do not exist is problematic: ongoing cases may render such conclusions premature or incorrect, and testing from other cases is often confined to facts unique to those cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Importing conclusions from co-pending cases is improper where the opposing party cannot examine testing circumstances or results; courts will scrutinize whether methodology underlying such imported conclusions is accessible and reliable. See United Services Automobile Ass'n v. Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., No. 2:18-cv-00366 (E.D. Tex. 2019).
